newsitem.title: JAPAN: Locals criticise slow reaction to Japan oil slick.
newsitem.headline: Locals criticise slow reaction to Japan oil slick.

text.p: Residents of Japan's oil slick-hit northern coast on Saturday accused authorities of reacting too slowly to the disaster, as the environmental and economic cost mounted.
The local economy is heavily dependent on the fishing industry and might be damaged by consumers' worries, a fisheries task force official said.

"Right now the battle is against damage to the fish, but the bigger fight will be against public relations damage as consumers shy away from seafood," said Satoshi Nomuru, head of Kyoto Fisheries Union Federation's task force.

Officials admit they have no idea how much oil from the Russian-registered 13,157-tonne tanker Nakhodka has been released. The 26-year-old tanker was carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of fuel oil when it broke up in stormy seas on January 2.
Wakasa Bay, where the cleanup is now focused, was crowded on Saturday with people still fishing off piers and surfers enjoying the waves.
Hatcheries teem with fish and shellfish beds are abundant around the picturesque seaside town.
But Maizuru's wholesale fish market, a normally bustling central sales point for the region, was empty on Saturday, save for hundreds of crows perched forlornly around the marketplace.

"I can't see how the Maritime Safety Agency didn't take earlier action beyond monitoring the slicks. It's not like they don't have recent experience with oil spills," said a local fisherman, who declined to be identified.
In January 1990, a Hong Kong-registered tanker ran aground just west of Maizuru and spilled 900 tonnes of oil (6,300 barrels) over seaweed and shellfish beds.
Many locals say the authorities should have been aware of the potential damage resulting from a larger spill.
Japanese authorities have in the past faced fierce public criticism for their slow reactions to disasters such as the 1995 Kobe earthquake, in which thousands of people died.
The area now hit by the spill is no stranger to environmental problems.

In December 1995, volatile sodium coolant burst from reactor pipes in Monju nuclear plant near Wakasa Bay. The plant remains closed and the official in charge of the plant committed suicide after a cover-up came to light.
